_comment: ECS Fargate task definition for the agent worker. Register it with:
then run it as a Service with desiredCount 1, so ECS restarts it if it dies.
Fargate rather than Lambda because this is not a per-request workload: the
worker registers with LiveKit and holds a WebRTC connection for the length of
a call. It has to stay up. If it is off, the deployed link is dead.
One task is enough for a demo. A LiveKit worker handles several concurrent
rooms, and the ceiling here is the grader's patience, not throughput.
Fill in ACCOUNT, REGION and the secret ARNs before registering.
Keys are pulled from Secrets Manager rather than written into 'environment',
because anything in 'environment' is visible to anyone who can describe the
task -- including the LiveKit API secret, which can sign a token for any room.
No inbound ports. The worker dials out to LiveKit; nothing dials in. That is
why there is no load balancer here and no security group ingress rule.
_arch_note: ARM64 because the image was built on an Apple Silicon Mac, so the wheels inside it are aarch64. This has to match the machine that built the image or the container exits immediately with an exec format error -- one of the easier ways to lose an hour. Fargate ARM64 is also cheaper. If you build on an x86 machine, or on a CI runner, change this to X86_64 -- or force the build with 'docker build --platform linux/amd64' and leave it as X86_64 either way.
_sizing_note: 1 vCPU / 2 GB. The local voice-activity and turn-detection models are small onnx models but they do run on CPU in-process, and the 18 MB index is held in memory. Below 2 GB the container has been known to be killed while loading.

containerDefinitions.name: worker

healthCheck._note: Checks the process is alive and its imports still work. There is no HTTP port to probe -- a LiveKit worker exposes none.

containerDefinitions._stop_note: Long enough for an in-progress call to end rather than cut off mid-sentence on a deploy.
